newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt holds ground, eyes 102 target.
newsitem.headline: German debt holds ground, eyes 102 target.

text.p: German debt held its ground in early trading on Friday, shrugging off U.S. market losses and convincing traders that a test of the psychologically key 102.00 level is possible before the weekend.

"It looks like this market just does not want to quit," said one trader, surprised that the German debt market has continued to rise despite all calls that it should move lower not higher in the near-term.
By 0746 GMT the September Bund futures contract, traded in Frankfurt, was up one basis point at 101.89, having moved between 101.75 and 101.99.
Meanwhile the 10-year cash bond was trading at 102.49 compared with the 102.40 close on Thursday.

Although U.S. Treasuries closed lower for the fourth straight session on Thursday, the German market appeared little impressed. "It is quite remarkable how well the German market has managed to de-couple from the U.S. market," a dealer said.

Fundamental reasons however seem to be playing a minor role in the market's strength which dealers said is currently based largely on technical factors. "I cannot see any new fundamental factors to lift the market, it is all technical trading now," another trader added.

Dealers explained that although short positions were put on several times during recent days, they are squeezed out in the afternoon. "It is was the same story all week, we were cautious, tried to put on some shorts and were squeezed out in the afternoon," a dealer said.
In light of these developments, dealers predicted Bunds could test the key psychological 102 level. And if that level were to give way, a very strong jump would be sure to follow.
On the other side, support is set around 101.80 and after that at 101.47.
Another related reason for the bond market's strength could be the fact that the year's half-year mark is approaching.

"There are a number of funds that are still too heavily invested in cash, and those players might be quite interested in piling into the bond market," predicted a dealer. But a number of dealers also said such interest might be short lived, which could open up floodgates for a stronger decline at some point in the future.
